title: Discovery: Defining Your Buy Box (Market, Property Type, Price Range, Goals)

slides.title: Write the buy box before you see listings, so you can walk away without debate
slides.subtitle: Lesson PA.1. Discovery: Defining Your Buy Box (Market, Property Type, Price Range, Goals)
meta: Education only. Not legal, tax, lending, or insurance advice.
slides.notes:
This is the first lesson of the acquisition phase. By the end of it, you'll have a written, one-page buy box.

That page ranks your goals. It states your constraints. It names your hard requirements. And it describes the property you want in terms someone else could search with. It ends with a pass rule, a sentence that tells you when to walk away from a listing without arguing about it. When I say pass in this lesson, I mean decline, as in "we'll pass on that one."

Why does this come before any market research? Because Sam's PA.2 and PA.3 lessons use this page. PA.2 picks a market with it. PA.3 builds your property pipeline with it.

We'll build Maya and Chris's buy box, then test it on Cedar Ridge at two prices. Every figure is an assumption. The Cedar Ridge ones are the ones the whole course uses, and new ones are marked. First, a few terms.

slides.title: The math in this lesson rests on eight terms, and each one is a plain idea
rows: A normal year and a bad year. Cedar Ridge's weak case: $265 a night at 50% occupancy, not $300 at 58%
Average nightly rate: what guests pay per booked night
Net operating income: booking revenue minus operating costs, before the loan payment
The yearly principal and interest on the loan
The full monthly payment: principal, interest, property taxes, insurance, and HOA dues
An upfront lender fee equal to 1% of the loan
A loan qualified mainly on the property's income compared with its payment (PA.6)
slides.notes:
Before we start, eight terms. You'll hear all of them in the worked example, so let's get them straight now.

STR is short-term rental. The base case is a normal year for a house, and the weak case is a bad year. For Cedar Ridge, the weak case is $265 a night at 50% occupancy, instead of $300 at 58%.

ADR is the average nightly rate. NOI, net operating income, is booking revenue minus operating costs, before the loan payment. Cedar Ridge's costs already include a 5% capital reserve.

Debt service, or P&I, is the yearly principal and interest on the loan. PITIA is the full monthly payment: principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and HOA dues.

A point is an upfront lender fee equal to 1% of the loan. And a DSCR loan is one the lender qualifies mainly on the property's income. PA.6 covers it in detail.

Two more you'll hear: cash to close is the down payment, closing costs, and points. Total cash in adds furnishing.

slides.eyebrow: What a buy box is for
slides.title: A buy box protects you from budget drift and from underwriting the wrong houses

left.head: Drift
left.note: Nobody decides to raise the budget. It happens one listing at a time.
items: You start looking for a three-bedroom house at $380,000.
A month later you're touring a $450,000 house with a pool, because the photos were good.

right.head: Wasted work
items: Reading rules, pulling comparable listings, underwriting, calling lenders.
Sam's PA.3 builds a pipeline of 5 to 10 qualified properties.
Without a buy box, qualified means nothing, and the pipeline fills with the wrong houses.

slides.notes:
A buy box is a search specification. It says what you'll buy, where, at what price, and under what conditions. Anything outside the box, you don't look at twice.

It protects you from two things.

The first is drift. You start looking for a three-bedroom house at $380,000. A month later you're touring a $450,000 house with a pool. The photos were great and the agent said it "books great". Nobody decided to raise the budget by $70,000. It just happened, one listing at a time.

The second is wasted work. Every property you seriously consider costs hours. Reading rules, pulling comparable listings (similar rentals nearby), underwriting, calling lenders. Sam's PA.3 builds a pipeline of 5 to 10 qualified properties. Without a buy box, "qualified" means nothing.

A good buy box is short and specific. You write it before you see listings. And it's hard to change on purpose. If you want to change it, you rewrite it, with numbers. You don't change it in a driveway during a showing.

slides.title: Your goals pull against each other, so rank them and let the top two or three decide
slides.text: Seven common goals: cash flow, long-term ownership, personal use, tax planning, portfolio growth, desired involvement, and safety.
rows: Your own peak-season week is a week you didn't rent
A deal bought for the depreciation can lose money monthly, and the deduction may be unusable
In 0.2, a co-host taking 18% of booking revenue turned $5,572 of cash flow into -$7,798
Stretching to buy again sooner leaves less reserve for this house
slides.notes:
Before you describe a property, rank your goals. People want several things from a short-term rental purchase, and they conflict. A ranking tells you which one wins when they do.

The common seven are cash flow, long-term ownership, personal use, tax planning, portfolio growth, how involved you want to be, and safety. Safety means protecting your household's savings and income if the house underperforms.

Here's how they fight. Personal use pulls against cash flow. Your own peak-season week is a week you didn't rent.

Tax planning can pull against everything else. A deal bought "for the depreciation" can lose money every month. And the deduction may not even be usable, depending on your household. Lesson 0.2 covered why.

Low involvement pulls against cash flow. In 0.2, a full-service co-host taking 18% of booking revenue turned Cedar Ridge from $5,572 a year to minus $7,798.

Portfolio growth pulls against safety. If you stretch now to buy again sooner, this house gets a thinner reserve.

Rank your goals 1 to 7. Only the top two or three shape the search. If two owners rank them differently, settle it now.

slides.title: Write down the limits you can't wish away; most of them come from your 0.3 scorecard
rows: Two caps: max cash to close, and max total cash in (plus furnishing). Total cap = savings minus reserves and other startup costs.
DSCR (qualified mainly on the property's income; PA.6), conventional investment, or both, with your planned down payment.
Driving hours. Distance decides whether you can fix a problem yourself or must pay someone.
The hours per week you'll actually give it, from 0.3.
The property reserve and emergency savings you won't spend below. These are floors, not targets.
slides.notes:
Constraints are limits you can't wish away. Most of them come straight from lesson 0.3.

Money comes as two caps. The first is the maximum cash to close: down payment, closing costs, and points, all due on closing day. The second is the maximum total cash in, which adds furnishing.

To find the total cap, start with your liquid savings. Take out your emergency savings and your property reserve. Then take out the other startup costs from your 0.3 cash stack. What's left is the most you can put in.

Why two caps? Furnishing comes after closing. And the cash-to-close cap stops a cheaper furnishing plan from turning into a bigger house. If your 0.3 scorecard carried a funding condition, write it here too.

Financing path. Write which loan types you'll pursue and your down payment. The lender decides eligibility later, in PA.6 and PA.7.

Distance, in driving hours. Time, in hours per week. And minimum reserves, which are floors you don't spend below.

slides.title: Describe the property in lines concrete enough for Sam's PA.2 and PA.3 filters
items: **Market type** and its demand driver: drive-to leisure, urban, event-driven, business travel.
**Property type:** detached, townhouse, condo, small multi-unit. It changes legality, lending, and insurance.
**Location inside the market.** Zoning, HOA boundaries, and permit caps can change street by street.
**Price range.** A floor screens out houses too small or worn. The ceiling comes from your money and downside rules.
**Capacity and amenities.** More beds can raise the nightly rate (ADR) and the wear. Water or height brings insurance questions.
**Operating complexity:** septic, wells, long private roads, snow, older systems. Each adds cost or response time.
slides.notes:
Now the property itself. Keep each line concrete enough that Sam's filters can apply it.

Market type: name it and its demand driver. Sam's PA.2 picks the actual market.

Property type matters for three reasons. Legality, because of condo and HOA rules. Lending, because some lenders restrict condos or certain property types. And insurance.

Location inside the market. Rules can change street by street. Zoning districts, HOA boundaries, and permit caps can all differ within one town. Write where you'll look, and where you won't.

Price range. You need a floor and a ceiling. The floor screens out houses too small or too worn to fit the rest of the box. The ceiling comes from your money constraints and your downside rule. It doesn't come from what sellers are asking. I'll show you how to calculate it shortly.

Guest capacity and amenities. More capacity can mean a higher nightly rate. It also means more wear, more cleaning, and more noise risk. Separate what guests expect from what adds complexity. Any amenity with water or height brings insurance and safety questions.

Operating complexity. None of these kills a deal alone. Decide how much you'll accept.

slides.title: A property must clear every hard requirement before it gets any more of your time

gates.q: Is unhosted STR use legal at the address, including HOA and deed rules?
gates.sub: Use SR.1; record the city or county source. (Airbnb also says check local rules: [article 1397](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/1397).)

gates.q: Is there a written STR insurance quote your underwriting can carry?
gates.sub: Platform protection is not a substitute (PA.12)

gates.q: Do the property type, location, and income fit a lender's written guidelines?
Are cash to close and total cash in at or under your caps?
Does the weak case stay inside your downside floor at a real loan quote?
gates.sub: A weak-case cash flow floor, plus a base-case NOI to debt service minimum

slides.notes:
Hard requirements are the lines a property must clear, every one, before you spend real time on it. They aren't preferences. Fail one, and you pass on it. That means you walk away.

Five belong in almost every short-term rental buy box.

One: legal STR use at the exact address. Unhosted means you don't live there during guest stays, and that use has to be allowed there. Any HOA or deed restriction has to allow it too. Use the SR.1 checklist and record the city or county source. Airbnb itself tells hosts to check local laws and HOA rules, but Airbnb isn't the source.

Two: acceptable insurance. That means a written quote at a premium your numbers can carry.

Three: lender fit, in writing.

Four: your two cash caps. No exceptions because the house is great.

Five: minimum downside performance. Set a floor on weak-case cash flow after debt service, and a minimum ratio of base-case NOI to debt service.

Add a sixth if 0.3 surfaced one. For Maya and Chris, the deal must work with self-management.
slides.end: Plus any requirement from your 0.3 scorecard. Maya and Chris: it must work with self-management.

slides.title: The pass rule has four parts, and it allows the box to change only in writing

nodes.d: Or a price over your ceiling that the seller won't bring down
Over the ceiling? Offer at or under it first. If the seller won't accept, pass.
In writing, new numbers, signed by every owner. Never during a showing.

box.label: Why log every pass
box.text: After 20 passes you'll see a pattern. If every house in your range fails the insurance quote, that's information for Sam's PA.2 market choice, not a reason to lower your standards.

slides.notes:
The pass rule is one or two sentences you agree on in advance. It tells you what to do when a listing doesn't fit.

A good one has four parts. The trigger: any failed hard requirement, or a price over your ceiling that the seller won't bring down. The action: pass. A listing above the ceiling can still get an offer at or under the ceiling. If the seller won't accept it, pass. The record: log which requirement failed. And the change process: the buy box changes only on purpose, in writing, with the new numbers, signed by every owner. Never during a showing.

Why log every pass? Because after 20 passes you'll see a pattern. Maybe every house in your price range fails the insurance quote. That's information. It goes back to Sam's PA.2 market choice. It isn't a reason to lower your standards.

The log also stops you from re-reading the same bad listing three times because it keeps showing up in your feed. You already decided. The log says why.

slides.title: Maya and Chris rank safety first, cash flow third, and tax planning only fifth
rows: Emergency fund stays at $51,000; property reserve stays at 6 months of PITIA, the full payment
Favor durable houses and stable rules over a short-term price opportunity
Base-case NOI minus debt service stays positive
Drive time matters; personal days go in slow weeks
Tie-breaker only; no deal is bought for depreciation
Not before Sam's OP.10 review and the OP.11 decision on a second property
slides.caption: Cash flow and desired involvement share rank 3: self-managing about 2.7 hours a week (assumption, from 0.3) is how the cash flow stays positive.
slides.notes:
Maya and Chris are the couple this course follows: two earners with $210,000 in savings. Cedar Ridge is a hypothetical lake house listed at $399,000. In PA.8 they agree to buy it at $385,000. In real life they'd write the box first and meet the house later. I'm showing both so you can see the box work.

Number one is safety. The $51,000 emergency fund stays put, and the property reserve stays at six months of PITIA.

Number two is long-term ownership, a hold of 10 years or more. That's an assumption.

Number three is cash flow while they self-manage. They put desired involvement here too, because self-managing is how the cash flow stays positive.

Number four is personal use, about 10 days, off-peak. That's why drive time matters.

Tax planning is fifth, a tie-breaker only. Portfolio growth is last. They won't consider a second property before Sam's OP.10 review and the OP.11 decision.

slides.title: Their $145,000 cap is what savings leave after reserves and startup costs

lines.label: Other startup costs from the 0.3 stack

slides.side:
Funding date: $210,000 today + 4 months x $3,500 saved = $224,000. They round the result down to a **$145,000** cap.

Today, the same math leaves **$131,044**. The 0.3 funding condition covers that gap: no offer until the stack is funded.

side_box.label: Why a separate $115,000 cap
side_box.text: $145,000 - $32,000 furnishing = $113,000, already under $115,000. It only binds if furnishing drops below $30,000.

slides.notes:
Where does the $145,000 cap come from? Start with savings and take out everything that has to stay untouched.

Today Maya and Chris have $210,000. Take away the $51,000 emergency fund and the $15,342 property reserve, and $143,658 is left. That's already under $145,000. Their 0.3 stack also has $12,614 of other startup costs: the punch list, inspections, permits, and two launch months. Take those out, and $131,044 is left. So today they can't fund the cap.

That's the job of the funding condition from 0.3. They save $3,500 a month for four months, which gets them to $224,000. Run the same subtraction and you get $145,044. They round down to $145,000.

The $115,000 cash-to-close cap doesn't bind for them. $145,000 minus $32,000 of furnishing leaves $113,000, already under it. It would only take over if they cut the furnishing budget below $30,000. That's what it's for: a cheaper furnishing plan shouldn't become a pricier house.

slides.title: Their two cash caps set a price ceiling of $393,000 on the DSCR terms

lines.label: Cash to close as a share of price

result.label: Box ceiling: the tighter cap wins

slides.side: Caps (assumptions): **$115,000** max cash to close and **$145,000** max total cash in. $145,000 - $32,000 furnishing = $113,000.

side_box.label: The downside rule is tighter for Cedar Ridge
side_box.text: Its weak case hits -$6,000 at about $392,000. For this house, that's the limit.

slides.notes:
Now the money constraints become a price.

On the DSCR terms, cash to close is 25% down plus 3% closing costs. That's 28%. Then one point. A point is 1% of the loan, and the loan is 75% of the price. So the point is 0.75% of the price. Cash to close is 28.75% of the price.

Now divide. The cash-to-close cap: $115,000 divided by 28.75% is $400,000. The total-cash-in cap: $145,000 minus $32,000 of furnishing is $113,000. Divide by 28.75% and you get $393,043.

The tighter cap wins. Their box ceiling is $393,000 contract price on these terms.

The downside rule gives another ceiling, but only for a specific house, because it depends on that house's revenue. For Cedar Ridge, the weak case reaches minus $6,000 at about $392,000. The lowest ceiling wins, so for this house the limit is about $392,000. At $392,500 it would fail hard requirement 5.

slides.title: Their buy box fits on one page: a detached 3 to 4 bedroom lake house under $393,000
rows: Drive-to lake leisure market (Sam's PA.2 picks it); within 2.5 hours of home and 10 minutes of lake access
Detached single-family; no HOA, or HOA with written STR permission; no condos. 3 to 4 bed, 2+ bath, sleeps 6 to 8
$325,000 to $393,000 contract price; DSCR at 25% down, with a conventional quote for comparison
Parking for 3 cars, reliable internet, outdoor space, year-round road access
No pool; hot tub only if the insurer quotes it; septic and well accepted with inspection and water test; punch list under $4,000
Weak-case cash flow after debt service no worse than -$6,000 a year; base NOI / debt service at least 1.20
Legal STR use; written insurance quote at or under $3,500 a year; lender fit in writing; self-management with a named cleaner plus backup
Pass on any failed requirement. Over $393,000: offer at or under it, and pass if the seller won't accept. Log it. Change only in writing, signed by both.
slides.notes:
Here's the whole buy box on one page.

Market: a drive-to lake leisure market, within 2.5 hours of home and a 10-minute drive of lake access. Sam's PA.2 picks the actual market.

Property: detached single-family. No HOA, or an HOA with written permission to host. No condos. Three to four bedrooms, sleeps six to eight.

Price: $325,000 to $393,000. The floor is their judgment call. It screens out houses too small or worn to fit.

Limits: no pool. A hot tub only if the insurer quotes it. The punch list, the small repairs before guests arrive, stays under $4,000.

The downside rule is theirs, not a lender's. Minus $6,000 a year is about $500 a month they could cover from salary. And 1.20 means NOI is at least 20% above the loan payment, a cushion before cash flow turns negative.

And the pass rule, written out so neither of them has to argue later.

slides.title: At $385,000 Cedar Ridge clears every number, with four evidence checks pending
rows: 3 bed, 2 bath, sleeps 8, no HOA, drive-to lake market
$3,200 a year in the model; written quote needed
Named local cleaner plus backup still to line up
slides.notes:
Now we test the box. First, Cedar Ridge at the $385,000 contract price.

Cash to close is $110,688, under the $115,000 cap. Total cash in is $142,688, under $145,000. Both clear.

In the weak case, NOI is $18,162. Debt service is $23,637 a year: a $288,750 loan at 7.25% over 30 years. So the weak case loses $5,475, better than the minus $6,000 floor.

Base-case NOI is $29,209. Divide by $23,637 and you get 1.24. That's above 1.20.

Property fit is a yes.

Four checks are pending. Insurance: the model uses $3,200, under their $3,500 cap, but a model isn't a written quote. Legal use is an address-level check with PA.2 and SR.1. Lender fit needs a written answer in PA.6. And self-management needs a named local cleaner plus a backup.

So Cedar Ridge clears every number. "Pending" doesn't mean it clears. Those rows stay open until the evidence arrives.

slides.title: At the $399,000 asking price, the same house fails three hard requirements
slides.text: Same revenue and operating costs. Property tax scales with price at 1% (assumption).

box.label: What made the deal
box.text: Negotiating $399,000 down to $385,000. If the seller had refused, the pass rule says walk (PA.8).

slides.notes:
Now the same house at the $399,000 asking price. Revenue and operating costs stay the same. The only change is property tax, which I scale with price at 1%. That matches the example's $3,850 on $385,000.

Cash to close is $114,713. That passes, barely.

Total cash in is $146,713. That's over the $145,000 cap. Fail.

The weak case now loses $6,475 a year. That's worse than the minus $6,000 floor. Fail.

Base NOI to debt service drops to 1.19. That's under 1.20. Fail.

Base-case cash flow is still positive, $4,572. That's why people talk themselves into houses like this. The base case looks fine. The box says no.

So the same house fails three hard requirements at asking price. The $14,000 negotiation from $399,000 down to $385,000 is what makes Cedar Ridge a deal for Maya and Chris. If the seller had refused to go below $399,000, their pass rule says walk. PA.8 covers how to set that walk-away price before you're emotionally attached.

slides.eyebrow: Test 3 · A house to walk away from
slides.title: A $435,000 house with a pool fails the cash caps before anyone looks at revenue

lines.label: List price, 4 bed with a pool (hypothetical)
Cash to close as a share of price
Cash to close, against a $115,000 cap

result.label: Total cash in, vs. a $145,000 cap

slides.side:
It also has a pool, which is outside their complexity limit. An offer at $393,000 wouldn't fix that.

Logged as: **over cash cap; pool.** No underwriting needed.

side_box.label: The value of the box
side_box.text: The $435,000 house never takes an evening of their time.

slides.notes:
Here's the third test, and it's the one I like best, because it's so short.

A four-bedroom house with a pool comes up in the same market, listed at $435,000. It's hypothetical.

On their DSCR terms, cash to close is 28.75% of the price. That's $125,063, already over the $115,000 cap. Add $32,000 of furnishing, and total cash in is $157,063, over the $145,000 cap.

It also has a pool, which is outside their complexity limit. Even an offer at their ceiling wouldn't fix the pool.

So they pass and log it as "over cash cap; pool". They don't pull comparables. They don't build a revenue model. They don't call the lender.

That's the value of the box. The $435,000 house never takes an evening of their time.

When you're in your own search, you'll feel the pull of houses like this. That's exactly when the one-line log entry earns its keep.

slides.title: Fill in your constraints from your statements and your 0.3 cash stack
rows: Total liquid, excluding retirement, at your funding date
Lender months x PITIA, or your higher target
Most you'll pay on closing day
Any gap still to close before an offer
slides.notes:
Now your turn. The full template has seven sections, A to G: goals, constraints, price ceiling, property description, hard requirements, pass rule, and a pass log. Fill it in and save it as one page.

This slide is section B, your constraints. Most of it comes from your 0.3 work.

Liquid savings, excluding retirement, as of your funding date. Your emergency savings floor. Your property reserve floor, the lender's months times PITIA or your own higher target. Then the other startup costs from your 0.3 cash stack, the full list of cash a purchase needs.

Now subtract. Savings minus those three lines is your max total cash in.

Max cash to close is the most you'll pay on closing day. It only matters if it's lower than your total cap minus furnishing.

Then any funding condition from line 1 of your 0.3 scorecard, the cash stack line. Financing terms, drive time, and hours per week finish it.

If you can't fill in a row, that's useful. It tells you what to get first.

slides.title: Compute your price ceiling three ways and use the lowest one
rows: Cash to close as % of price
Max cash to close / line above
From the PA.4 model for each house you underwrite (leave blank until PA.4)
Lowest of the lines filled in
slides.notes:
Section C turns your caps into a price.

First line: cash to close as a percentage of price. That's your down payment percentage, plus closing costs, plus points times the loan percentage. For Maya and Chris it was 28.75%.

Second line: your cash-to-close cap divided by that percentage.

Third line: your total-cash-in cap, minus furnishing, divided by the same percentage.

Fourth line: the ceiling from your downside rule. You can't fill that in yet. It comes from Sam's PA.4 model, house by house. Leave it blank for now.

Your price ceiling is the lowest of the lines you've filled in. For Maya and Chris, that was $393,000, and about $392,000 for Cedar Ridge itself.

Then finish the rest of the page. Section D is the property description. Section E is your hard requirements, each with the evidence you need and who confirms it. Section F is your pass rule, written in one or two sentences. And section G is the pass log: date, address, which requirement failed, and whether a price change would fix it.

That last column matters. It tells you which passes might come back if the seller drops the price.
slides.caption: Then finish the page. D: property description. E: hard requirements, with evidence and who confirms. F: your pass rule in one or two sentences. G: the pass log.

slides.title: The city, your insurer, your lender, and your CPA each confirm one part of the box
rows: Unhosted STR use is allowed at the address. Use SR.1; an STR attorney if unclear.
For each address that passes your other filters
Premium and exclusions for STR use on the house
For each finalist, before the diligence window
Property type, location, and planned use fit the loan, and the terms in section C
Before you rely on your ceiling
Before you put tax planning in your top three goals
slides.notes:
Here's who confirms what for the buy box.

The city or county licensing office confirms that unhosted short-term rental use is allowed at each address that passes your other filters. Use the SR.1 checklist. If the answer is unclear, go to an STR attorney. Don't take a listing agent's word for it.

Your insurance agent confirms the premium and the exclusions for STR use on each finalist. Do that before the diligence window, the period after your offer is accepted when you inspect and verify. If insurance fails, you want to know before you've paid for inspections.

Your lender confirms that the property type, location, and planned use fit their loan. They also confirm the terms you used in section C. If the real terms are different, your price ceiling changes. Recompute it.

And your CPA. Talk to them before you put tax planning in your top three goals. That way the ranking reflects your household's actual situation, not a hope about depreciation.

Every "confirm with" line is a phone call or an email. Keep the replies with your buy box.

slides.title: Four short tasks give you a signed, one-page buy box before Sam's PA.2
items: Rank your seven goals 1 to 7. If there are two owners, rank separately, then agree on one list.
Fill in section B and compute your price ceiling in section C.
Describe the property (D), write your hard requirements and pass rule (E, F), and have every owner sign.
Start the pass log with the first listing you see that fails a requirement.
slides.next: Next: what to bring from Sam's **PA.2 to PA.5** (next slide). Then I pick up at **PA.6, DSCR Loans 101: How They Qualify the Property, Not You.**
slides.notes:
Four tasks. Most take an evening.

First, rank your seven goals. If there are two of you, rank them separately first, then compare. The places you disagree are the conversation you need to have now, not at the offer.

Second, fill in section B, your constraints, and compute your price ceiling in section C. Leave the downside-rule line blank until PA.4.

Third, describe the property in section D: market type, location, property type, size, price range, and limits. Then write your hard requirements and your pass rule, one or two sentences. Then have every owner sign the page. A signature sounds formal. It's what makes the box hard to change in a driveway.

Fourth, start the pass log. The first listing you see that fails a requirement goes in, with the reason.

Then take the page into Sam's lessons. The next slide shows what to watch for in each one.

slides.title: Carry the buy box through Sam's PA.2 to PA.5, then bring the financing line to PA.6

Use your pass rule as the filter; keep the pass log
Test your downside rule on a real listing; fill in section C, line 4
The tax timing from 0.2, in detail
Your financing line becomes a written quote

slides.notes:
Here's how the buy box travels through the next four lessons, which are Sam's demos. I won't re-teach them. Here's what to watch for and what to bring back.

In PA.2, Choosing a Market for Ownership, check whether each market Sam screens allows unhosted STR use at all. The address-level check comes later, house by house. Note which markets fit your drive time and price range.

In PA.3, Deal Sourcing, Sam shows how to fill a pipeline of 5 to 10 qualified properties. Your pass rule is the filter. Keep the pass log going the whole time.

In PA.4, Reading a Full Underwriting Package, your downside rule gets tested on a real listing. This is also where you fill in line 4 of your price ceiling.

In PA.5, Cost Segregation and Year-One Depreciation, you'll see the tax timing from 0.2 in detail. In Maya and Chris's box it ranks fifth. It's not a reason to buy.

After those four, I pick up with PA.6, DSCR Loans 101. There, the financing line in your buy box becomes a written lender quote.

items.title: Airbnb Help Center, General info about hosting places to stay (article 1397)
items.note: hosts should check local laws and HOA or co-op rules before hosting

slides.text:
